flag: Purchasing-power-parity (PPP) comparisons carry an error of several points. The OECD figure (EU gap 26%) and the Eurostat index (28%) differ by 2 points on the same year for this reason.

The direction of the gap over time depends on the measure. Since 2019 the gap widened on OECD constant-price GDP per head (28% to 31%) and on the Eurostat index (25% to 28%), but narrowed on OECD current-price GDP per head (30% to 26%). Since 2015 the Eurostat index (32% to 28%) and the current-price series (36% to 26%) narrowed, constant-price widened (29% to 31%). The constant-price series is a growth fact (real GDP per head since 2019: EU +4%, US +10%); the current-price narrowing coincides with relative price changes (not verified) and the Eurostat 2019 to 2024 move is about 2 points, inside PPP error. The card quotes real growth and both current-price windows and says the trend is not settled.

FOR THE EDITOR, not in the card. OECD US row: HRSPOP = 860.4 hours per head, but EMP x HRSAV / POP = 825.4 (4.2% lower); all 13 other areas reconcile. Editor check of the OECD file: total hours HRSTO 2024 = 292,630.3 million (2023: 291,066); HRSTO / POP = 860.4 = HRSPOP; HRSTO / EMP = 1,775 hours per worker; GDP per hour (GDPHRS) divides GDP by the same HRSTO, so GDP per hour and hours per head are consistent on the 860 basis. HRSAV (1,702) is the odd series, probably a different employment or per-job concept. 860 is the primary basis; GDP per head and the EU gap (26%) do not depend on it. Sensitivity if the persons-based 825 were right (US GDP per hour 104.4): EU productivity share of the gap about 82% instead of 69%, EU hours gap about 5% instead of 9%, Belgium output per hour about 104 instead of 109, Belgium hours gap about 17% instead of 21%. Direction of every conclusion is unchanged (Belgium at or above the US per hour; EU gap mostly output per hour).
If US hours per worker are quoted anywhere use 1,775 (HRSTO / EMP), not HRSAV 1,702. Because HRSAV is inconsistent, Denmark's hours per worker are not compared with the US in the card.
Log shares of the gap are blank where one term is above and the other below the US (Belgium, Netherlands, Denmark): the split is not meaningful there.

Belgium's output per hour is flattered by selection: 43% of the population is employed against 48.5% in the US (persons basis), so fewer lower-productivity workers are in the denominator. More people in work would probably lower average output per hour.

EU employment per head (48.6%) equals the US (48.5%), so for the EU as a whole the hours gap is hours per worker, not fewer people in work. Fewer people in work applies to Belgium (43%), France and Italy.
Ireland is left off chart 1 but is inside the EU bar. Excluding it the OECD EU gap is 27.1% instead of 26.0%.

Ireland's GDP per head is 164 (US = 100) in the OECD data, inflated by multinationals' booked profits. Shown in outputs, left off chart 1. Its Eurostat consumption index (99, EU = 100) is a better guide to living standards.
Consumption (AIC) gap uses 2023 because the US 2024 value is empty in the Eurostat extract. GDP gap uses 2024. Different years, so the two gaps are not strictly comparable.

AIC counts health and education provided by government at cost. The US spends much more per head on health. Whether that is higher living standards or higher prices is not tested here, so the 35% consumption gap may overstate the gap in what households can enjoy.
All figures are averages per head. Nothing here measures the median household, inequality, poverty or health. The US has higher average income partly because its top is richer (not tested here).

Fewer hours per head mix choice (more holiday, shorter weeks) and constraint (fewer people in work). The OECD data do not separate the two. The employment-rate split is not used because of the US identity issue above.

The EU figure averages very different countries: Poland is at 58 and the Netherlands at 98 (US = 100) in GDP per head. 'Europeans' as one group hides this. EU27 is the current 27 members; the UK, Switzerland and Norway are outside it.
Current-price GDP per head in USD PPP is computed as GDP per hour x hours per head. It is not read directly from a GDP per capita series.
Data pulled 2026-11-15; the OECD API could not be re-queried during review. 2024 is the latest year in both sources. OECD figures for 2024 may be provisional and revised.
